title: Empress Of - Breaking and Entering
summary: Lorely Rodriguez, aka Empress Of, is a Latin American musician from Los Angeles. Lorely joins Breaking And Entering to chat to fill-in host Charlie Miller about the strong voices that shaped her life growing up, as well as her latest album Us. Us is a much more collaborative piece of work than her debut Me. Lorely filled the writing process with people she loves, and musicians that inspire her, creating a sense of community and ‘a way to deal with how crazy the world is’.
transcript:
Lorely Rodriguez, who records as Empress Of, joined fill-in host Charlie Miller in the Triple R studio in December 2018 to discuss her second album, Us. They spoke about community, the voices that shaped her singing and finding a wider range of emotions in her music. Edited for length and clarity.

Charlie: Empress Of is Lorely Rodriguez, who is right across from me. How are you today?

Lorely: I'm really good. I took a nap because I have jet lag.

Charlie: I don't think I've mentioned that you're from Los Angeles.

Lorely: I'm from Los Angeles. My name is Lorely. I have a project called Empress Of. You just heard my song, 'Just the Same'. You also just heard a song I made when I was in college.

Charlie: Oh, for real?

Lorely: Yeah, one of the Colorminutes that you played.

Charlie: I was not sure. I thought you were referring to 'Just the Same'.

Lorely: No, 'Just the Same' I wrote yesterday. I mean, not yesterday.

Charlie: Theoretically speaking.

Lorely: Yeah, it feels like yesterday.

Charlie: Going back to Colorminutes, I love that title. It literally refers to the box of colours they were uploaded with and the time, but it seems almost like conceptual art.

Lorely: It was. It was the first bit of music I made as Empress Of. I don't know if you're familiar with Tierra Whack. She's an American artist, and this year she put out an album of like 30 one-minute songs or something. I was like, sick, somebody else is doing it. It was a way of making the initial Empress Of demos. I gave myself an exercise of writing one-minute songs every day, and a few of those were adapted into the EP that came afterwards, Systems, my first EP.

Charlie: You were living in New York for a few years, but it was an intense place, and you're now back in LA.

Lorely: Have you ever been to New York? It's crazy.

Charlie: Everyone outside America is constantly updated with images of New York. Even if you haven't been there, you can kind of feel it and smell it.

Lorely: And it smells kind of rank.

Charlie: It's grungy.

Lorely: I lived in New York. It was my training ground as an artist, playing in warehouses. I finished my debut album there, Me. When I put it out, I was like, all right, cool, I'm done. I'm good, New York, see ya. I'm moving back to LA, where I'm from, born and raised. I just wanted to be really close to my family.

Charlie: It's probably nice to keep it as somewhere you can visit and not have to live.

Lorely: I was there last week, and it was nice to visit. I was like, cool, visit, air quotes, visit. I don't live here, and it feels really great just to visit.

Charlie: Spending time back in East LA, right?

Lorely: Yeah.

Charlie: I can imagine a lot of noise and music in the streets.

Lorely: I love sound. I like cities that are noisy. I was walking through Melbourne today, and I had that feeling, wow, this is a noisy city in a good way. I was in the downtown area at an intersection, and the little click, click, click on each corner, the cars going by and all the tourists. I was like, wow, this is a hustly-bustly city. I had that feeling, okay, this is how I'll remember Melbourne this trip, from those sounds.

Charlie: I think it's important that cities are noisy. There seems to be a trend in urban development to stamp out noise and take away public space, where communities living in those spaces are being forced to lower the noise. You've alluded in songs to gentrification and how it's affecting communities. Since you moved back to LA, does it feel different to when you were growing up?

Lorely: Oh my gosh, yeah, for sure. I hang out in places my mother would cry if I went to when I was young. Now there's coffee shops everywhere, and you can buy a really nice pencil holder made out of clay. Just stuff like that, little trinket shops and coffee shops. But where I live, it's an in-between point.

What I love about LA is it reminds me of my Latino culture so much. My parents are from Honduras, and I grew up with salsa playing out of cars and sound systems, cumbia, merengue, eating tacos, rice and beans and stewed meats. That's part of the neighbourhood I live in.

Charlie: And that's still a big presence?

Lorely: It's still a big presence. It feels like home. I feel grounded. I'm reminded constantly of who I am, which is something I was missing living in New York. My heritage, I miss that.

Charlie: The album's titled Us, and it's a big collaborative project. A sense of community was important in recording it. How is friendship, as a way of uniting in a time with so much alienation, significant to you?

Lorely: For me it was more a way to deal with how crazy the world is, how we're constantly bombarded by politics, especially American politics, because everything's crazy right now. I wanted to retreat into a safe place with people I love. It's a way of dealing with that. I made my debut totally alone, produced, wrote, recorded it. I wanted to work with other artists, be in the room and have conversations about music, make music with other artists. I wanted to be close to my family and inspired by other artists in LA. That's part of the whole process of the record.

Charlie: Is that a process you've enjoyed and might want to continue?

Lorely: I enjoyed it, for sure. I don't know about the future, because I have a feeling I'm going to be one of those artists that doesn't repeat the same thing twice. I tried to make Us all by myself, and it wasn't sounding the way I wanted it to, so I leaned into my community.

Charlie: I've read you're a big fan of Björk and Elizabeth Fraser from Cocteau Twins. That's part of why I played Susana Baca's cover of 'The Anchor Song'. When you first started singing, how did those powerful voices influence your approach? Your own vocal style is elaborate.

Lorely: I started singing quite young. I was in choirs, and I grew up listening to really powerful voices. My mom has a really loud voice. She can scream my name from far away and I'll hear it. I've had strong voices throughout my upbringing. I grew up listening to Mariah Carey and Céline Dion, big divas. When I started illegally downloading music, I discovered artists like Björk, Imogen Heap and Regina Spektor. When I was 14, I was like, whoa, these ladies are doing such strange things. I was really inspired by that. I love discovering how people make their own way in music.

Charlie: Occasionally you sing in Spanish. You've said it's a confessional approach to songwriting that takes a different form to writing in English. Can you see it continuing to be something you go to when you need to express something too difficult otherwise?

Lorely: I've always written music in Spanish, since my first EP, Systems, which was half in English and half in Spanish. I see it more as part of my culture and who I am. It feels natural as a third way of expressing a feeling, a time or a place. I have English, Spanish and music as the languages I use to make art. I've done that since I started making music, and I think I'll always do that.

Charlie: Maybe a fourth form, because you've directed a music video now?

Lorely: 'When I'm With Him'. Visuals are a new thing I'm learning how to do and gaining more confidence in. I directed my first music video, 'When I'm With Him', and I've been taking control of the visuals. I knew what I wanted for the cover and all the press photos. I wrote all the treatments for the videos, and I'll keep doing that.

Charlie: It's an exciting trend I've seen, particularly in the States, artists taking on their own music video production. It's a way of controlling more than just the music.

Lorely: Initially it came out of necessity, because I had a really small budget and was like, there's no way I'm going to be able to do this. But meeting with directors, talking to them about my videos and how I want to represent myself, I realised I could do that myself. I probably know how to represent myself the best.

Charlie: On the new record, you've talked about an emotional balance from song to song, darker and lighter moments. Are you feeling confident now, as opposed to the harder time releasing Me in 2015?

Lorely: I learned a lot from releasing my debut and playing it, how it looks, how it sounds, how it made me feel. With Us, for this record, I can't say for the next one, I really wanted a spectrum of emotions. I wanted to play on stage and have highs and lows, and feel even. I don't know if that makes sense.

Charlie: I think so.

Lorely: I have a wider range of emotions, and I didn't want to focus on one thing to trap myself into.

Charlie: Honesty and being true to yourself are important in your songwriting. What weight do you put on that, as opposed to creating a persona?

Lorely: It's funny, because I technically have a persona. Empress Of is a veil. It's my armour. It's how I present myself to everyone, but I'm kind of one and the same. When I write my songs, I really need to believe them. I know a song is good and it's done when I can convince myself that the feelings are real. It is very much me. I am Empress Of. I just put a different name on it.

Charlie: Thanks so much, Lorely Rodriguez, for coming into Triple R.

Lorely: Thank you for having me.
